They're usually made by small studios with big aspirations. They have a pretty hard time adding new content because they need to implement the survival features everyone expects like crafting, while still making it unique to the 30 other unfinished survival games

Easy to make with modern game engines, already proven popular with the 13 - 19 age bracket and is pretty reliable for youtube hits. Combine this with a well understood design using a techtree/gathering mechanic that acts like a MMORPG but without the RNG (although some add some back in).

This gameplay is very condusive to an early access model as you can simply add in content at different points in the existing tech tree without being too disruptive to people's current game state. Sort of like "Hey there's a new higher tier of furnace! Now I can build this new one where my old one is and be more effective!".

I could go on, but the reality is that it's a popular genre that is somewhat of a perfect storm for a small developer hoping to make a game on a continuous small income.

It takes a long time to make an open world survival game, since you have to design a massive world, create the textures and models of various things to fill it and spend an equally lengthy amount of time finding and fixing bugs. And all that time spent is time the game isn't available for people to play, and hence not available for Let's Players and other e-celebrities to market.

Oh, and they're also often pretty expensive to make. Pre made models and things can help there, but it's still going to take a while (and hence a lot of paid hours) to get a game like ths to completion.

If you release the game in early access, you can:

  1. Rely on the community to find the bugs, making it easier (and quicker) to fix them.

  2. Get feedback on where your game is/isn't working.

  3. Have well known Youtube users make videos of the game while its still in progress, getting its name out more than you would be able to if you waited till it was done to release it.

  4. Make money off the game before it's done.

It might also be because other games (like Minecraft) were released in a beta state and steadily improved over time. So this has sort of become the unofficial 'ritual' for titles folllowing in their footsteps.
